title: Cycling Calories by Distance: Kcal Estimates
description: Estimate calories burned over a cycling distance with Cycling Calories by Distance — from rider weight and distance, clearly approximate. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, under the simple model this page uses, a 170 lb rider covers 30 miles at roughly 40 kcal per mile — about 1,200 kcal for the ride, before hills argue.
quick_answer: Cycling Calories by Distance estimates the energy a ride costs from the rider's weight and distance covered. Enter both and read an approximate kilocalorie figure for the ride — a planning estimate built on a stated model, honest about everything it leaves out: hills, wind, speed and the rider's engine.

A consistent estimate, applied the same way every ride, is what a log needs. Precision matters less than the same ruler each time.
The bike commute's calorie figure is the one part of its cost that pays you. Priceless — but here, quantified.
Distance-based estimates set expectations honestly: riding burns real energy, and the number is smaller than the appetite it creates. Plan with the figure, not the feeling.
170 lb rider, 30 miles, at the model's roughly 40 kcal/mile: ≈ 1,200 kcal. Ride it into a headwind or up a pass and the truth is higher — the model is the floor of the story, labelled as such.
100 km (62.1 mi) at the same rough rate: ≈ 2,485 kcal. A metric century is a day's eating on top of a day's eating, which is why century riders plan food like logistics.

popular_table.note: Treat the table as an order of magnitude with a signpost: your power meter, if you have one, outranks any model — kilojoules of work ≈ kilocalories of food energy is the cyclist's useful coincidence.

faq: Does this replace a specialist tool or professional measurement?
No. It is a simple distance-and-weight estimate. A power meter measures actual work; a lab measures actual metabolism. This is the planning figure for riders who have neither.
Is my input uploaded?
No — weight and distance are used in your browser for the estimate and go nowhere else.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Traffic does not burn calories; hills and wind do, and the simple model omits them — ride the estimate as a floor.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Roads wind, and cyclists ride roads. Use the ridden distance — calories follow the wheels, not the crow.
Can route results change over time?
Your fitness does, happily. The model is fixed so your log stays comparable; the rider improves against it.
Do heavier riders really burn more?
Yes — moving mass costs energy, especially uphill and accelerating. Weight is in the model for exactly that reason.
What about e-bikes?
Assistance subtracts rider work by an amount only the assist level knows. Treat the estimate as the unassisted equivalent and discount it by feel.
Does speed change the estimate?
In the simple model, barely — distance and weight carry it. In truth, faster riding burns more per mile into the wind; treat fast rides as above the estimate.
Why do apps give different numbers?
Different models: some price heart rate, some power, some speed bands. Consistency inside your own log beats consensus among apps.
Calories in or out — is this net?
It is an estimate of energy expended on the ride. What you eat back is a separate, usually larger, number.
